zufft

Overview

zufft provides fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) for R, along with discrete cosine and sine transforms (DCTs and DSTs). It’s designed to replace fftwtools, without the need for FFTW:

  • fft_c2c() computes the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), like stats::fft().
  • fft_r2c() computes the DFT of real input and returns only the non-negative frequency terms. fft_c2r() is its inverse.
  • fft_dct() and fft_dst() compute DCTs and DSTs of types 1 to 4.
  • fft_stats() and mvfft_stats() are drop-in replacements for stats::fft() and stats::mvfft().

The names will be familiar if you’ve used fftwtools. The conventions for axes, normalisation and the DCT and DST definitions follow scipy.fft. Helpers such as fft_next_len(), fft_freq() and fft_shift() mirror SciPy’s next_fast_len(), fftfreq() and fftshift().

zufft bundles the BSD-licensed FFT code of ducc0, the same files and commit that SciPy uses. This means you don’t need a system FFTW library: install.packages() is all it takes, on every platform. zufft is MIT-licensed and carries no GPL code.

It’s also fast. With CRAN’s build, zufft is faster than fftwtools on 30 of 33 benchmark cases, and at most 1.26 times slower on the other three. Threads help further.

Installation 

# Install zufft from CRAN:
install.packages("zufft")

# Or the development version from GitHub:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")

Usage 

library(zufft)

fft_c2c() computes the full spectrum, just like stats::fft():

x <- c(1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7)
fft_c2c(x)
#> [1]  27+0.000000e+00i  -5+5.196152e+00i   0+4.440892e-16i -11+0.000000e+00i
#> [5]   0-4.440892e-16i  -5-5.196152e+00i

For real input, the spectrum is Hermitian-symmetric: the negative-frequency terms are the complex conjugates of the positive ones. fft_r2c() returns only the n %/% 2 + 1 non-negative frequency terms, and fft_c2r() takes you back. Give n to recover an odd length: by default fft_c2r() assumes an even one, as SciPy’s irfft() does:

X <- fft_r2c(x)
X
#> [1]  27+0.000000e+00i  -5+5.196152e+00i   0+4.440892e-16i -11+0.000000e+00i
fft_c2r(X, n = length(x))
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

Use axes to choose the dimensions to transform, and workers to spread the work over several threads. Here we transform each column of a matrix on two threads:

m <- matrix(rnorm(4096 * 64), 4096)
spec <- fft_r2c(m, axes = 1, workers = 2)
dim(spec)
#> [1] 2049   64

R stores arrays in column-major order, so the first dimension is contiguous in memory. That’s why, with axes = NULL, the real transforms halve the first dimension (to n %/% 2 + 1): it’s fast, and it matches fftwtools. If you give axes explicitly, the last axis listed is halved instead, as in SciPy. The results are bit-identical whatever the number of threads.

fft_dct() and fft_dst() compute DCTs and DSTs with SciPy’s definitions. The default is type 2, and the inverse takes you back to x:

fft_dct(x, norm = "ortho")
#> [1] 11.0227038 -4.6508890 -1.0000000  0.4082483  0.0000000 -3.8343924
fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

Lengths with only small prime factors transform fastest. fft_next_len() returns the smallest fast length at or above n, so you can zero-pad the input to it:

fft_next_len(1009)
#> [1] 1024

Coming from fftwtools or scipy.fft

vignette("migrating-from-fftwtools") maps every fftwtools function to its zufft equivalent. The main thing to remember is scaling: zufft scales inverse transforms by 1/n, as SciPy does. Use norm = "none" if you want the unscaled inverse that fftwtools and stats::fft() return.

If you’re coming from Python, the scipy.fft article covers the other side. The definitions match, and the test suite checks zufft against SciPy on 2040 cases.

Speed

You don’t need a native build for zufft to keep up with fftwtools. The table below compares the two on a Linux x86-64 runner, using one thread. fftwtools uses Ubuntu’s FFTW, which is built with SSE2 and AVX SIMD code. The numbers come from bench/RESULTS.md.

Case fftwtools zufft, CRAN build ratio zufft native, ratio
1-D complex 1 048 576 27.02 ms 20.64 ms 0.76 0.59
1-D real 1 000 000 16.50 ms 11.77 ms 0.71 0.57
columns real 1024 × 1024 5.97 ms 2.55 ms 0.43 0.34
2-D complex 2048² 279.85 ms 67.76 ms 0.24 0.19
3-D complex 128³ 44.80 ms 34.10 ms 0.76 0.83
1-D complex 100 000 1.44 ms 1.81 ms 1.26 0.83

A ratio below 1 means zufft is faster. With CRAN’s portable build (SSE2), zufft is faster on 30 of the 33 benchmark cases. It’s slower on three: single 1-D complex transforms of about 10^5 to 10^6 points. Unlike the columns of a matrix, a single transform can’t be split into independent 1-D transforms. The worst of these is 1.26 times slower. Built for the local CPU (AVX2 here, see Native build), zufft is faster on all 33. Each ratio compares runs on the same machine, but the two builds ran on separate runners.

Where does the speed come from? Most of it comes from planning. zufft caches its plans, while fftwtools creates a new FFTW plan (with FFTW_ESTIMATE) and destroys it on every call. Threads add more (workers = 2), which fftwtools doesn’t offer. And every length runs in O(n log n), even a prime one: a prime length of 100 003 takes milliseconds, compared with seconds for stats::fft().

On Apple silicon the gap is wider. That’s partly because Homebrew’s FFTW has no SIMD code for double precision there: FFTW’s NEON support is single precision only. You’ll find those numbers in bench/RESULTS.md too.

Native build

CRAN’s binaries are compiled to run on any CPU of their architecture. On x86-64, that means SSE2, whose SIMD registers hold two doubles. If your CPU has AVX2 or AVX-512, a build for your own machine runs faster. It takes two steps in R:

  1. Set the environment variable ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS with Sys.setenv(). zufft adds it to its compiler flags, and no other package sees it.

  2. Install from source with install.packages(..., type = "source"). A prebuilt binary, which is what you get by default on macOS, is already compiled and ignores the variable.

Sys.setenv(ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS = "-march=native") # "-mcpu=native" on Apple silicon
install.packages("zufft", type = "source")

If you want the development version, clear pak’s cache first. Otherwise pak reuses a cached build of the same commit, which ignores the variable:

pak::cache_delete(package = "zufft")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")

You can check the result with zufft_info(). The SIMD width, in doubles, is 4 with AVX2, 8 with AVX-512, and 2 for a portable build:

zufft::zufft_info()$simd_width

This works on Linux and macOS. Installing from source needs a compiler (on macOS, the Xcode command line tools). Windows builds ignore ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS and stay portable, because code built for AVX by the GCC in Rtools crashed in our tests.

How much does it help? On the Linux x86-64 runner of bench/RESULTS.md, where this gives AVX2, the 16384 × 64 complex column case drops from 15.39 ms to 9.17 ms. A complex transform of prime length 10 007 drops from 659.6 µs to 389.5 µs. On Apple silicon the SIMD width stays at two doubles (NEON), so a native build (-mcpu=native there) gains little.

There are two things to keep in mind:

  • The package then runs only on CPUs like yours, so don’t copy the installed library to other machines.

  • With GCC on a CPU with fused multiply-add (FMA), results can differ in the last bit between thread counts. zufft::zufft_info()$fp_contract reports "fast" when that applies. CRAN’s builds report "off".

Licence

zufft is MIT-licensed. Its bundled ducc0 files are the “BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-or-later” subset that SciPy vendors, used under BSD-3-Clause. inst/COPYRIGHTS lists every copyright holder. No GPL-only ducc0 code is included.
